title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 34
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Money That Was Never There
passages.text:
A. Banking began as storage and became something else almost immediately. A person with coin to protect deposited it with someone who had a strong room, and received a receipt. The receipt could be transferred to settle a debt, which meant the claim circulated while the coin stayed where it was, and at that moment the deposit had become money without anyone deciding that it should.

B. The decisive discovery was that depositors do not all return at once. A holder of many deposits observes that the quantity withdrawn on any day is small and predictable, and can therefore lend most of what is held while remaining able to meet ordinary demands. This is the mechanism by which lending creates deposits rather than merely transferring them, and it is the reason banking is productive and inherently fragile in the same breath.

C. The fragility has a specific and unusual shape. A bank that has lent well is still unable to meet all its depositors at once, because the loans cannot be recalled at the speed the deposits can be demanded. A belief that others are withdrawing is therefore a reason to withdraw regardless of whether the bank is sound, and the belief can be self-fulfilling — a failure mode that does not require anyone to have made a bad loan.

D. Central banking developed as an answer to that specific problem rather than as a general plan. An institution able to lend to a solvent bank against good collateral during a panic removes the incentive to run, and the promise to do so is more valuable than the lending itself, since a credible promise means it is rarely needed. Much of what looks like intervention is the maintenance of a belief.

E. The difficulty with that arrangement is that it changes behaviour in advance. A bank confident of support has reason to take risks it would otherwise avoid, and the profits from doing so are private while the consequences are partly public. Every subsequent regulatory apparatus — capital requirements, liquidity rules, supervision — exists to constrain a behaviour created by the remedy for the earlier problem.

F. What has changed most recently is where the activity sits. Functions that were once conducted by banks now occur in institutions that lend, borrow short and transform maturity without holding a banking licence, and the same fragility follows the activity rather than the label. Regulation attached to institutions rather than to functions has repeatedly discovered that the risk moved somewhere the rules did not.

passages.title: What Noise Takes
passages.text:
Hearing depends on cells that do not regenerate, and every consequence of noise exposure follows from that single fact. Sound reaching the inner ear moves fluid, which bends microscopic hair cells arranged along a spiral membrane, and each region of that spiral responds to a particular range of frequencies. Damage those cells and the loss is permanent: no treatment restores them, and no interval of quiet regrows what has gone.

The pattern of loss is characteristic and diagnostic. Cells responding to higher frequencies are the more vulnerable, so damage typically appears first as a notch in the upper range that the person does not notice — high frequencies carry little of the energy of speech. What is lost early is the information distinguishing consonants from one another, which is why the first complaint is usually not that sounds are quiet but that speech is hard to follow when other people are talking.

That distinction matters because it explains why amplification disappoints. A hearing aid makes sound louder, and the difficulty is not principally that sound is too quiet but that the ear has stopped separating one sound from another. Devices have improved substantially at processing rather than merely amplifying, and the residual gap between hearing aided and hearing intact is a limit of the damaged ear rather than of the electronics.

Two exposures cause damage and they are usually confused. A single very loud event can destroy cells outright, which is intuitive; more damage in total is done by moderate exposure sustained over years, which is not. Occupational noise below the level anyone would call painful, experienced for a working life, produces measurable loss, and the dose that matters is intensity multiplied by duration rather than intensity alone.

Prevention is entirely effective and almost entirely neglected. Protection worn correctly prevents the damage completely, costs very little, and requires the person to act against an absence — nothing hurts, nothing is immediately harder, and the loss it prevents will arrive decades later in a form easy to attribute to age. Interventions that engineer the noise down at source work better than those requiring individual compliance, for the same reason that applies wherever this comparison has been made.

The wider effects have moved from anecdote to evidence and change how the subject should be framed. Hearing loss is associated with social withdrawal, with reduced participation, and with a measurably higher risk of later cognitive decline, and while the causal pathways are still being established the association is consistent and substantial. Treating it as a minor inconvenience of ageing understates it in a way the data no longer support.

passages.title: Paying Somebody Else Not To
passages.text:
A carbon offset is the purchase of a claim that an emission somewhere else did not happen, and the entire question of whether it works is a question about a counterfactual. The seller must establish what would have occurred in the absence of the payment, which is not observable, and every difficulty in the market descends from that irreducible fact rather than from any particular failure of administration.

Additionality is the name of the central problem. A project that would have gone ahead anyway sells a reduction that did not occur because of the purchase, and the buyer's payment changes nothing in the atmosphere. Establishing additionality requires demonstrating that the project was not financially viable unaided — a claim about intentions and finances that a project developer is strongly motivated to make and an assessor poorly placed to disprove.

Forest projects illustrate the specific difficulties best because they combine several. Protecting a forest from clearance that was planned generates credits; if the clearance simply moves to another forest, the atmospheric effect is nil while the credits remain saleable, and this displacement is hard to detect and easy to omit. A forest's carbon is also reversible, since it can burn or be cut later, and a credit sold as permanent against a stock that is not permanent is a promise about the future backed by nothing in particular.

Measurement is more tractable than the accounting and is often blamed for its failures. The carbon in a stand of trees can be estimated with reasonable accuracy from sampling and remote sensing; what cannot be measured is the baseline against which the saving is claimed. Repeated investigations have found projects whose measurement was adequate and whose baseline was implausible, which is the combination that produces credits that are real in the ledger and absent in the atmosphere.

Removal and avoidance are routinely sold as equivalent and are not. Paying for carbon to be taken out of the air and stored durably is a different transaction from paying for an emission not to occur, and the second is what most cheap offsets are. A market that prices them identically, while they differ sharply in how durable the effect is and in how confidently either can be verified, will supply the cheap one, which is what has happened.

None of this makes the underlying idea worthless, and the collapse in confidence has been about as indiscriminate as the earlier enthusiasm. Paying for reductions where they are cheapest is sound in principle, and specific project types with measurable, non-reversible, clearly additional effects survive scrutiny. What has failed is the use of a weakly verified credit to describe an activity as neutral, which was always a claim about accounting rather than about the atmosphere.
